screens.title: Recap: Gene Therapy Mechanisms
screens.html:
QUICK REVIEW

Recap: Gene Therapy Mechanisms

Before we dive into specific disorders, let's refresh how we get the DNA where it needs to go.

Gene Augmentation: Adding functional gene copies to cells with broken versions.

Gene Inhibition: Inserting genes to stop faulty ones from creating harmful proteins.

screens.title: Viral Vectors: The Delivery Vans
screens.html:
🧠

Viral Vectors: The Delivery Vans

Viruses are nature's best hakers; they are evolved to inject their genetic material into host cells. In gene therapy, we remove the viral disease-causing genes and replace them with the therapeutic human DNA.

Remember

Vectors must be highly specific, non-toxic, and capable of avoiding the patient's immune response.

screens.title: CLINICAL APPLICATION
screens.html:
CLINICAL APPLICATION

Case Study: Cystic Fibrosis (CF)

CF is caused by a mutation in the CFTR gene, leading to thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and digestive system.

Targeting the lungs is ideal for gene therapy because vectors can be delivered directly via an aerosol spray (nebuliser).

screens.title: The CF Gene Therapy Challenge
screens.html:
⚠️

The CF Gene Therapy Challenge

The Goal

Deliver a functional CFTR gene to the epithelial cells lining the lungs so they can correctly pump chloride ions.

The Obstacle

The thick mucus layer itself acts as a barrier, preventing the viral vectors from reaching the cell surface.

Watch out

Lung cells turn over frequently, meaning the treatment often needs to be repeated.

screens.title: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency
screens.html:
Severe Combined Immunodeficiency

Often called 'Bubble Boy disease', SCID is a group of rare disorders caused by mutations in genes involved in the development and function of T and B cells.

Without a functional immune system, simple infections can be fatal. Gene therapy offers a chance to 'reboot' the system.

screens.title: Treating SCID-X1
screens.html:
Treating SCID-X1

Step 1: Harvest

Stem cells are removed from the patient's bone marrow.

Step 2: Transfection

A retrovirus inserts the functional gene into the stem cells in a lab.

Step 3: Infusion

The corrected stem cells are infused back into the patient to grow a new immune system.

screens.html:

👍​

👎​

screens.title: SCID-X1 Risks
screens.html:
SCID-X1 Risks

Early gene therapy trials for SCID-X1 were halted because some patients developed leukaemia.

👍​

Why is that?

a) The patients' bodies rejected the new T-cells as being foreign tissue, causing an inflammatory storm.

b) The retroviral vector inserted the new gene near an oncogene, accidentally switching on cancer-causing pathways.

screens.title: NEUROGENETICS
screens.html:
NEUROGENETICS

Targeting the Brain: Huntington's

Unlike CF, Huntington's Disease (HD) is caused by a dominant 'gain-of-function' mutation. The presence of the mutant protein is what kills neurons.

Therapy here uses RNA Interference (RNAi) or antisense oligonucleotides to 'silence' the faulty gene rather than replace it.

screens.title: Why Expression Fails
screens.html:
Why Expression Fails

Challenges in Long-term Use

Getting the gene in is easy; keeping it 'switched on' is the real challenge.

Epigenetic Silencing

Cells may identify foreign DNA as viral and shut it down via methylation.

Immune Response

The body may destroy cells producing novel proteins it does not recognize.

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

Somatic vs. Germline Therapy

Somatic Therapy

Targets body cells (lung, blood).

Effects remain with the patient.

Ethically accepted for treating disease.

Germline Therapy

Targets eggs, sperm, or embryos.

Changes are heritable.

Controversial; banned in many nations.

screens.title: The Germline Debate
screens.html:
The Germline Debate

We are the first species in history that has the power to direct its own evolution. — Unknown

If we could eliminate Huntington's from a family tree forever, should we?

screens.title: Laboratory Biosecurity
screens.html:
Laboratory Biosecurity

Viral vector research requires strict biosecurity to prevent accidental release. Facilities are regulated by the OGTR (Office of the Gene Technology Regulator).

1

Containment - Physical barriers like HEPA filters and airlocks.

2

Attenuation - Vectors engineered to prevent replication outside the lab.

screens.title: Ethical Considerations
screens.html:
Ethical Considerations

Equality of Access

Gene therapies are exceptionally expensive (sometimes millions of dollars per dose).

Genetic Enhancement

Where is the line between 'curing a disease' and 'enhancing a trait' (like height or muscle mass)?

screens.title: Safety Fail-Safes
screens.html:
🔍

Safety Fail-Safes

To prevent 'off-target' effects, scientists are developing 'Genetic Kill Switches'.

Example

A suicide gene can be included in the vector. If the cell starts behaving abnormally (turning cancerous), the patient can be given a specific drug that activates the suicide gene, killing only the modified cells.

screens.title: The Road Ahead
screens.html:
The Road Ahead

Gene therapy is moving away from simply 'adding' genes towards Gene Editing using CRISPR-Cas9.

This allows for precise 'Search and Replace' functionality within the existing genome, reducing the risk of accidental cancer.

screens.title: Regulatory Oversight in WA
screens.html:
Regulatory Oversight in WA

In Western Australia, all gene therapy trials must undergo rigorous ethical review by institutional boards and federal regulators.

Informed Consent: Patients must understand all risks.

Pre-clinical Testing: Extensive animal trials before humans.

screens.title: Biological Warfare & Biosecurity
screens.html:
Biological Warfare & Biosecurity

The same technology used for healing could theoretically be used to create 'super-pathogens'. This 'Dual-Use' dilemma is why international biosecurity treaties are so strict.

screens.title: The Cost of a Cure
screens.html:
🤯

The Cost of a Cure

Traditional medicine manages symptoms over a lifetime. Gene therapy is a 'one-and-done' event.

Fun fact

Zolgensma, a gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy, costs roughly AUD $3 million per dose, making it one of the most expensive medicines in the world.

screens.title: Final Ethical Debate
screens.html:
Final Ethical Debate

Under what circumstances should germline gene therapy be permitted?

Consider a family with a terminal dominant disorder

versus the risk of creating designer babies.

screens.title: Final Ethical Debate
screens.html:
Final Ethical Debate

You might have said...

Arguments for: Eliminating suffering for all future generations; reduced long-term healthcare costs.

Arguments against: Consent (unborn children cannot consent); potential for 'genetic elitism' or eugenics; unknown long-term ecological impact on the human gene pool.

✅​

screens.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS
screens.html:
KEY TAKEAWAYS

🧠

Summary & Next Steps

Vectors (like viruses) are used to deliver functional genes.

SCID and CF are prime targets for gene augmentation.

Huntington's requires gene silencing techniques.

Ethical and safety concerns remain the biggest hurdles for widespread adoption.

Remember

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Compare in vivo and ex vivo gene therapy and explain one reason to choose an ex vivo approach.
steps: In vivo therapy delivers genetic material directly into the patient’s body or a target tissue.
Ex vivo therapy removes cells, modifies them outside the body and returns selected suitable cells.
Ex vivo modification can permit checks or selection before return, but requires accessible cells that can survive the procedure.

bank.q: Which best describes ex vivo gene therapy?
o: Cells are modified outside the body and returned
A drug is always injected directly into a tumour
Every cell in the body is replaced
bank.why: Ex vivo approaches modify cells outside the body before returning suitable cells to the patient.

bank.q: What is the aim of gene inhibition?
o: Reduce harmful gene expression or activity
bank.why: Inhibition strategies aim to reduce the effect of an unwanted or harmful gene product.

bank.q: How does in vivo delivery differ from ex vivo delivery?
o: Genetic material is delivered directly into the body
It never uses a delivery system
It occurs only in a laboratory dish
bank.why: In vivo delivery occurs directly in the patient; ex vivo modification occurs outside the body.
